title: Passover: a seat at the seder
hookLine: the seder opens with an invitation: let all who are hungry come and eat

cards: You met the seder plate on day four. Tonight, imagine you're the one who was invited. A friend's family, a partner's grandparents, a community seder in a rented hall.

You sit down, someone hands you a little book, and before anyone has eaten a thing, the leader lifts the flat bread and says, in Aramaic, an old invitation. This is the bread of affliction that our ancestors ate in Egypt.
Let all who are hungry come and eat. Before the story, the seder opens the door. Today: what it's like to walk through it.

teach.b: Ha lachma anya is said near the start of the seder, in Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews when it took shape, so that anyone listening would understand the invitation.

The whole night is built for people who don't know it yet. The book is the Haggadah, the telling, and many have English beside the Hebrew. People take turns reading, and it's fine to read your part in English.
It's long, and dinner comes after a lot of the story, so many guests eat a little something first.

teach.h: A BOOK, FOUR CUPS, AND LEANING.
teach.b: There are four cups, and grape juice counts. People lean to the left as they drink, the way free people once reclined at a feast.
When the ten plagues are named, people dip a finger or a spoon and take out a drop of wine for each one; many explain that a cup of joy is made less full when others suffer.

teach.h: DROPS FOR PLAGUES, A HIDDEN MATZAH.
teach.b: A piece of matzah, the afikoman, gets hidden, and children hunt for it. Later the door is opened for the prophet Elijah, with a cup poured for him. The songs at the end can get loud.
And questions are welcome all night; the Haggadah even makes room for the one who doesn't know how to ask. A practical note: in many homes there's no bread, cake or regular baked goods all week.
If you'd like to bring something, ask first. Flowers are always safe.

how: Many Jewish families invite friends, partners, neighbors and people who would otherwise be alone to the Passover seder; guests read along from the Haggadah, often in English, and are welcome to ask questions all night.

games.why: a drop for each plague. many explain it as a cup of joy made less full, because even an enemy's suffering isn't cheered.

practice: Picture a long table, set for more people than usual, with a chair for someone who hasn't arrived yet, and the leader lifting the matzah: all who are hungry, come.
Think of one person who might not have anywhere to be on a holiday, or a Friday night, or just a Tuesday, and hold them in mind. If you pray, you can pray for them; if not, wish them a full table.

wordCard.voice: Ha lachma anya. This is the bread of affliction: the Aramaic words over the matzah that open the seder with an invitation to anyone hungry.

carryVoice: Your line: all who are hungry, come. A night about freedom starts by making room at the table. See you tomorrow.
